catalog_quote: Stress is fully contrastive in Tetun; e.g. /'kabas/ 'cotton, thread, yarn' versus /ka'bas/ 'shoulder', /'kaben/ 'marry' versus /ka'ben/ 'saliva'. Nevertheless it falls most commonly on the penultimate syllable; e.g. /ha'karak/ 'want', /ka'miza/ 'shirt'. Final stress occurs in both native and loaned items; e.g. /ha'ris/ 'bathe', /si'nal/ 'sign'. Antepenultimate stress is much less common and is found only in a small number of Portuguese loanwords; e.g. /'mediku/ 'doctor', /a'merika/ 'America'. Unstressed vowels are always short, as are non-final stressed vowels; e.g. [a'merika] 'America', [ha'karak] 'want'. However, all vowels, regardless of height or quality, are regularly lengthened in stressed monosyllables and stressed final position; e.g. /'hat/ ['ha:t] 'four', /ka'bas/ [ka'ba:s] 'shoulder', /ha're/ [ha're:] 'see'. new_statements.rule_in_words: Default/regular stress on the penultimate syllable of the word. A minority of native words carry final stress with a lengthened final vowel (kabás 'shoulder', harís 'bathe', haré 'see'); the same author's Peace Corps course (p. xvii fn. 1) and Albuquerque 2011 / Greksáková 2018 treat these as final double vowels (kabaas, haree), under which analysis native stress is exceptionlessly penultimate (by vowel/mora count) and only Portuguese loans deviate. Antepenultimate stress exists only in a small set of Portuguese loans (médiku, siénsia), and many speakers regularise loans to penultimate. PL-528 itself labels stress 'fully contrastive' because it writes the final long vowels as single stressed vowels; hence reading fixed: penultimate syllable with lexical exceptions rather than free stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: PL-528: compounds have a single primary stress like single words (sec. 4.4.1). Albuquerque 2011 sec. 6.3.1: in some reduplications/compounds a secondary stress falls on the penult of the first member, primary stress on the (penult of the) last member. Nothing on rhythmic secondary stress in long words.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress in some native and loan words (kabás, kabén 'saliva', harís, sinál) with vowel lengthening; antepenultimate stress only in a few Portuguese loans (médiku, Amérika, siénsia, régua); unstressable clitics/particles (la 'not', preposition ba, ó '2sg'); laós with stress on o or level stress; loan stress often shifted to penult by speakers with little Portuguese (Albuquerque 2011 p. 92; Greksáková 2018 p. 311; Avram 2021 p. 93). Possible marginal vowel-length contrast flagged as needing investigation (PL-528 p. 12).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation forms (phonemic transcriptions of isolated words); orthographic convention marks non-penultimate stress with an acute accent. Compounds form one stress domain with a single primary stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted sources describe Tetun Dili = Tetun Prasa (tetu1246, ISO tdt), the Portuguese-influenced lingua franca of Dili, as distinct from Tetun Terik/Fehan (tetu1245). PL-528 and the Peace Corps course say 'Tetun' but explicitly mean Tetun Dili; Albuquerque 2011 and Greksáková 2018 use 'Tetun Prasa'. Greksáková's PDF is held under the tetu1245 folder held by the project but its ch. 7 phonology is Tetun Prasa (tetu1246). Avram 2021 sec. 9 opens 'In Tetun Terik' but the cited pages and examples are Tetun Dili (apparent slip).

The HathiTrust open_url returned an automated-access block 'Just a moment' 403 on both attempts (pt and ssd endpoints), so the listed copy could not be opened; the ANU open-repository copy (hdl 1885/146149, CC BY-SA 4.0) of the same printing was already held by the project and was read. It agrees with the catalog's penultimate rule and refines it: stress is lexically contrastive with a penultimate default, final stress in native and loan words, antepenultimate only in Portuguese loans, allophonic length on stressed final/monosyllabic vowels, single prima…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Penultimate stress is the default ('Most Tetun words have penultimate stress', p. 7), but stress is lexically contrastive: minimal pairs exist, final stress occurs in native and borrowed words, and antepenultimate stress occurs in a few Portuguese loans. The grammar marks non-penultimate stress with an acute accent for this reason. Vowel length is allophonic: stressed monosyllables and stressed final vowels are lengthened, all other vowels short.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described. On compounds the grammar says: 'Phonologically, such compounds have a single primary stress just as single words do.' (p. 22). Some compounds show reduction of the initial member (lo(k)raik 'afternoon' from loro-kraik). The negator laos/lahos is said to carry 'either stress on the /o/, or relatively equal stress on the two vowels'.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress in native and loaned items (/ha'ris/ 'bathe', /si'nal/ 'sign', Timór 'Timor'); antepenultimate stress only in a small number of Portuguese loans (/'mediku/, /a'merika/); rising diphthongs /ei ai oi ui au eu/ count as single vowels for the penultimate rule (kadeira, ideia), and where such sequences are not diphthongal penultimate stress is written (saúde); the preposition ba is unstressable while verb/deictic ba can be stressed; the general negator la is unstressable.
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Tetun Dili (Tetun Prasa), the Dili urban/lingua-franca variety, as distinct from the Fehan and other rural Tetun (tetu1245) varieties; no dialect narrower than Tetun Dili is singled out for the stress statement.

sources.note: p. xv: 'On native Tetun words, stress is always on the second-last syllable; e.g. Uma, haTEne, haREe.' p. xvii 'Stress and long vowels': most words stressed on the penultimate syllable; some words stressed on the last vowel, spelled as double vowels (haree 'see' vs hare 'rice', kabeen 'saliva' vs kaben 'marry'); some Portuguese-origin words stressed on the third-last syllable (siénsia). Footnote 1: unclear whether final long vowels in Tetun Dili are one syllable or two (ha.ree vs ha.re.e); in Tetun Terik evidence favours two, making stress consistently penultimate.
